claim: DILI is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the western world.
source: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the western world (Bernal and Wendon, 2013; Tujios and Lee, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bernal and Wendon, 2013 and Tujios and Lee, 2018

claim: DILI occurs at a rate of 19.1 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: Although it is rare (19.1 cases per 100,000 inhabitants), it is a major cause of drug withdrawal due to its associated morbidity and mortality (Leise et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leise et al., 2014

claim: DILI is a major cause of drug withdrawal due to its associated morbidity and mortality.
source: Although it is rare (19.1 cases per 100,000 inhabitants), it is a major cause of drug withdrawal due to its associated morbidity and mortality (Leise et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leise et al., 2014

claim: 50% of drugs with a black box warning for hepatotoxicity contain a mitochondrial liability.
source: This is supported by the fact that 50% of drugs with a black box warning for hepatotoxicity also contain a mitochondrial liability, with many associated specifically with iDILI (Dykens and Will, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dykens and Will, 2007

claim: Haplogroups have been associated with specific adverse drug reactions and drug efficacy.
source: Not only have associations between specific haplogroups and mitochondrial function been determined, but haplogroups have also been associated with specific adverse drug reactions and drug efficacy (Jones et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al., 2021a

claim: Mitochondrial genotype-specific responses to drugs are present at the haplogroup level in platelets.
source: In previous research, we have circumvented this issue by using freshly isolated platelets as a model system, demonstrating that mitochondrial genotype-specific responses to drugs are present at the haplogroup level (Ball et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ball et al., 2021

claim: HepG2 cells remain valuable as one of the most commonly used preclinical cell lines for the in vitro assessment of DILI.
source: Despite limitations regarding physiological relevance, HepG2 cells remain valuable as one of the most commonly used preclinical cell lines for the in vitro assessment of DILI (Weaver et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weaver et al., 2020

claim: Haplogroup H is the most common haplogroup in the UK.
source: Haplogroup H was selected for study as it is the most common haplogroup in the UK (Eupedia, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eupedia, 2016

claim: Haplogroup J is characterized by non-synonymous mutations in regions of the mitochondrial genome that encode respiratory complex I.
source: Haplogroup J, on the other hand, is less common in the UK but is characterized by non-synonymous mutations in regions of the mitochondrial genome that encode respiratory complex I.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about haplogroup J

claim: Haplogroup J is reported to be more susceptible to mitochondrial toxins.
source: Although no studies have specifically reported on iDILI and mitochondria haplogroup, haplogroup J is also reported to be more susceptible to mitochondrial toxins (Ghelli et al., 2009; van Oven and Kayser, 2009; Eupedia, 2016; Strobbe et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghelli et al., 2009; van Oven and Kayser, 2009; Eupedia, 2016; Strobbe et al., 2018

claim: Flutamide is a non-steroidal antiandrogen for the treatment of prostate cancer with a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.
source: Flutamide, a non-steroidal antiandrogen for the treatment of prostate cancer, has a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and is a known inhibitor of mitochondrial complex I (Coe et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coe et al., 2007

claim: Flutamide is a known inhibitor of mitochondrial complex I.
source: Flutamide, a non-steroidal antiandrogen for the treatment of prostate cancer, has a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and is a known inhibitor of mitochondrial complex I (Coe et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coe et al., 2007

claim: 2-hydroxyflutamide is the primary human metabolite of flutamide.
source: 2-hydroxyflutamide, is the primary human metabolite of flutamide and is a known inhibitor of both respiratory complexes I and II.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about flutamide metabolism

claim: 2-hydroxyflutamide is a known inhibitor of both respiratory complexes I and II.
source: 2-hydroxyflutamide, is the primary human metabolite of flutamide and is a known inhibitor of both respiratory complexes I and II.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about 2-hydroxyflutamide mechanism

claim: The maximum serum concentration of 2-hydroxyflutamide in humans is 4400 nM.
source: In humans, the rapid first-pass metabolism of flutamide results in much higher maximum serum concentrations of 2-hydroxyflutamide than its parent compound (4400 nM vs 72.2 nM).
evidence: Stated as pharmacokinetic data

claim: The maximum serum concentration of flutamide in humans is 72.2 nM.
source: In humans, the rapid first-pass metabolism of flutamide results in much higher maximum serum concentrations of 2-hydroxyflutamide than its parent compound (4400 nM vs 72.2 nM).
evidence: Stated as pharmacokinetic data

claim: Tolcapone was withdrawn due to cases of liver failure.
source: Meanwhile, tolcapone, a catechol-o-methyl transferase inhibitor used to treat Parkinson's disease, was withdrawn due to cases of liver failure and is a known uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation (Olanow, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003; Olanow and Watkin.)
evidence: Supported by citations to Olanow, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003

claim: Tolcapone is a known uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Meanwhile, tolcapone, a catechol-o-methyl transferase inhibitor used to treat Parkinson's disease, was withdrawn due to cases of liver failure and is a known uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation (Olanow, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003; Olanow and Watkin.)
evidence: Supported by citations to Olanow, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003

claim: No significant differences in oxidative phosphorylation parameters were observed between haplogroup H and J cybrids at basal state.
source: No significant differences in oxidative phosphorylation parameters were observed between haplogroup H and J cybrids (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from mitochondrial stress test shown in Figure 2A

claim: Complex I-driven maximal respiration was significantly greater in haplogroup J cybrids compared to haplogroup H.
source: Complex I and II-driven maximal respiration were significantly greater in haplogroup J cybrids (complex I mean difference 2.46 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.4, 4.53], p=0.021; complex II mean difference 2.97 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.9, 5.04], p=0.006).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from complex activity measurements

claim: Complex II-driven maximal respiration was significantly greater in haplogroup J cybrids compared to haplogroup H.
source: Complex I and II-driven maximal respiration were significantly greater in haplogroup J cybrids (complex I mean difference 2.46 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.4, 4.53], p=0.021; complex II mean difference 2.97 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.9, 5.04], p=0.006).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from complex activity measurements

claim: Complex III and IV-driven respiration was not significantly different between haplogroups H and J.
source: Whereas complex III – and IV-driven respiration was not significantly different between haplogroups H and J.
evidence: Experimental data from complex activity measurements

claim: The introduction of foreign mitochondrial genome into cybrids can lead to the initiation of retrograde responses to the nucleus primarily via calcium signaling.
source: However, it has been noted that the introduction of the foreign mitochondrial genome into cybrids, can lead to the initiation of retrograde responses to the nucleus primarily via calcium signaling (Luo et al., 1997; Amuthan et al., 2002; Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 1997; Amuthan et al., 2002; Srinivasan et al., 2016

claim: Flutamide treatment resulted in a substantial, concentration-dependent decrease in ATP at concentrations ≥33 µM.
source: As expected, a substantial, concentration-dependent decrease in ATP was evident when cybrids were treated with ≥33 M flutamide, however, this decrease was not significantly different between haplogroup H and J cybrids (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental data from ATP content assay shown in Figure 3A

claim: The effect of flutamide on ATP was independent of cell death.
source: The effect on ATP was shown to be independent of cell death, as no significant lactate dehydrogenase [LDH] release occurred at any of the concentrations used (data not shown).
evidence: Experimental data from LDH release assay

claim: Spare respiratory capacity was greater in haplogroup H cybrids across the central concentrations of the flutamide dose-response curve, although this did not reach significance.
source: Spare respiratory capacity (SRC), was greater in haplogroup H cybrids across the central concentrations of the dose-response curve, although this did not reach significance (J vs H: SRC mean difference –1.37 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [–2.83, 0.09], p=0.063).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from extracellular flux analysis

claim: Proton leak was significantly greater in haplogroup J compared with haplogroup H following flutamide treatment.
source: Furthermore, proton leak (PL), a negative indicator of mitochondrial health, was significantly greater in haplogroup J compared with haplogroup H (PL mean difference 1.29 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.3, 2.27], p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from extracellular flux analysis

claim: 2-hydroxyflutamide is the major circulating form of flutamide when it is administered clinically.
source: 2-hydroxyflutamide is the major circulating form of flutamide when it is administered clinically.
evidence: Stated as established pharmacokinetic knowledge

claim: ATP-linked respiration was significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following exposure to 2-hydroxyflutamide.
source: However, indicators of drug-induced mitochondrial toxicity, ATP-linked respiration, and SRC (Figure 4D and E), were both significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following exposure to 2-hydroxyflutamide (J vs H: ATP-linked respiration mean difference –1.13 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [-2.02,–0.25], p=0.017; SRC mean difference –1.74 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [-3.22,–0.25], p=0.027).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from extracellular flux analysis shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: Spare respiratory capacity was significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following exposure to 2-hydroxyflutamide.
source: However, indicators of drug-induced mitochondrial toxicity, ATP-linked respiration, and SRC (Figure 4D and E), were both significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following exposure to 2-hydroxyflutamide (J vs H: ATP-linked respiration mean difference –1.13 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [-2.02,–0.25], p=0.017; SRC mean difference –1.74 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [-3.22,–0.25], p=0.027).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from extracellular flux analysis shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: Haplogroup J cybrids had significantly higher complex I activity than haplogroup H when treated with flutamide.
source: When treated with flutamide (Figure 5A and B), haplogroup J cybrids had significantly higher complex I activity than haplogroup H (J vs H: mean difference 2.15 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.42, 3.89], p=0.021).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from complex activity measurements shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Haplogroup J cybrids showed a steeper dose-dependent reduction in complex I activity by flutamide than haplogroup H.
source: However, despite an overall higher level of activity for complex I, haplogroup J cybrids showed a steeper dose-dependent reduction in their complex I activity by flutamide than haplogroup H.
evidence: Inference from experimental data comparing dose-response curves

claim: Flutamide did not significantly reduce complex II activity in either haplogroup.
source: In line with its known targets, flutamide did not significantly reduce complex II activity in either haplogroup, however, there was generally a lesser impact on haplogroup J cybrids(J vs H: mean difference 1.23 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.01, 2.47], p=0.051).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from complex activity measurements

claim: 2-hydroxyflutamide decreased the activity of complexes I and II in both haplogroups.
source: In line with the known mechanism, 2-hydroxyflutamide decreased the activity of complexes I and II in both haplogroups (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Experimental data from complex activity measurements shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: Haplogroup J cybrids demonstrated significantly greater maintenance of complex I activity following 2-hydroxyflutamide treatment.
source: Haplogroup J cybrids again demonstrated a significantly greater maintenance complex I activity (J vs H: mean difference 2.81 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.5, 5.13], p=0.023) and whilst complex II activity was generally greater in haplogroup J cybrids after treatment this did not reach significance (J vs H: mean difference 1.2 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [–0.33, 2.73], p=0.111).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from complex activity measurements

claim: Cellular ATP levels were significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following treatment with tolcapone.
source: Specifically, cellular ATP levels were significantly lower in haplogroup J cybrids following treatment with tolcapone (J vs H: mean difference –29.46%, 95% CI [–50.83%, –8.09%], p=0.012) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from ATP content assay shown in Figure 6A

claim: The effects of tolcapone on cellular ATP content were observed in the absence of cytotoxicity.
source: These effects on cellular ATP content were observed in the absence of cytotoxicity (i.e. no significant lactate dehydrogenase [LDH] release) at all the concentrations used (data not shown).
evidence: Experimental data from LDH release assay

claim: Haplogroup J is more susceptible to uncoupling by 2,5-hexanediol compared to haplogroups H and U.
source: This increased susceptibility of haplogroup J cybrids to tolcapone-induced depletion is in agreement with findings reported by Ghelli et al., 2009, in which a non-hepatic cybrid model was used to determine that haplogroup J (vs haplogroups H and U) was more susceptible to uncoupling by the neurotoxic metabolite, 2,5-hexanediol (Ghelli et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghelli et al., 2009

claim: No differences were apparent between haplogroup H and J in any of the bioenergetic parameters measured following tolcapone treatment.
source: However, no differences were apparent between haplogroup H and J in any of the bioenergetic parameters measured.
evidence: Experimental data from extracellular flux analysis

claim: Four cases of liver failure among 100,000 individuals taking tolcapone led to a black box warning and a switch to entacapone.
source: In the case of tolcapone, four cases of liver failure among 100,000 individuals taking the drug, led to a black box warning and a switch to entacapone an alternative in-class compound.
evidence: Stated as clinical/regulatory history

claim: Entacapone has been reported to be less efficacious than tolcapone.
source: However, as entacapone has been reported to be less efficacious than tolcapone, the ability to make the drug selection based on the personalized risk of iDILI, would be of great value (Rivest et al., 1999; Olanow, 2000; Watkins, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003; Olanow and Watkins, 2007; Lees, 2008; Longo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rivest et al., 1999; Olanow, 2000; Watkins, 2000; Benabou and Waters, 2003; Olanow and Watkins, 2007; Lees, 2008; Longo et al., 2016

claim: Bicalutamide was less potent than flutamide or 2-hydroxyflutamide in terms of cellular ATP content.
source: In line with previous work (Ball et al., 2016), results demonstrated that bicalutamide was less potent than flutamide or 2-hydroxyflutamide in terms of cellular ATP content (Figure 7A).
evidence: Experimental data from ATP content assay shown in Figure 7A, supported by citation to Ball et al., 2016

claim: Haplogroup J exhibited higher proton leak in both control and bicalutamide-treated cybrids.
source: No significant differences were evident between the two cybrid groups in parameters of mitochondrial function using XF analysis, however as was the case with flutamide and 2-hydroxyflutamide, haplogroup J exhibited higher proton leak in both control and treated cybrids (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: Experimental data from extracellular flux analysis shown in Figure 7B-F

claim: Entacapone induced a weaker decline in ATP levels compared to tolcapone.
source: Entacapone induced a weaker decline in ATP levels compared to tolcapone, with a 50% decrease not reached at the highest concentrations tested (Figure 8A), reflective of previous work demonstrating it to be less toxic to mitochondria (Kamalian et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental data from ATP content assay shown in Figure 8A, supported by citation to Kamalian et al., 2015

claim: Haplogroup H cybrids induced a significantly greater increase in spare respiratory capacity following entacapone treatment.
source: It is, therefore, of interest that haplogroup H cybrids induce a significantly greater increase in SRC activity (J vs H: mean difference –1.5 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [-2.79,–0.21], p=0.027).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data from extracellular flux analysis

claim: This study demonstrates that HepG2 transmitochondrial cybrids can be created to contain the mitochondrial genotype of any individual of interest.
source: Importantly, these studies demonstrate for the first time that transmitochondrial cybrids can be created in HepG2 cells to contain the mitochondrial genotype of any individual of interest.
evidence: Inference from successful generation of 10 cybrid cell lines from different individuals

claim: The process of generating cybrid cells has the potential to introduce additional cellular changes beyond the intended effects upon the mitochondrial genome.
source: However, a caveat should be noted, that the process of generating these cells, particularly the use of ethidium bromide and PEG, has the potential to introduce additional cellular changes in addition to the intended effects upon the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: Speculation about potential unintended effects of the cybrid generation process

claim: Haplogroup J cybrids display an increased susceptibility to tolcapone-induced decrease in ATP.
source: It has shown that haplogroup J cybrids display an increased susceptibility to tolcapone-induced decrease in ATP and to mitochondrial dysfunction induced by 2-hydroxyflutamide, which supports previous findings on the increased sensitivity of haplogroup J to mitotoxicants (Strobbe et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental data from ATP content assays, supported by citation to Strobbe et al., 2018

claim: Haplogroup J cybrids display an increased susceptibility to mitochondrial dysfunction induced by 2-hydroxyflutamide.
source: It has shown that haplogroup J cybrids display an increased susceptibility to tolcapone-induced decrease in ATP and to mitochondrial dysfunction induced by 2-hydroxyflutamide, which supports previous findings on the increased sensitivity of haplogroup J to mitotoxicants (Strobbe et al., 2018).
evidence: Experimental data from extracellular flux analysis, supported by citation to Strobbe et al., 2018

claim: Inter-individual variation in mitochondrial genotype can be a factor in determining sensitivity to mitochondrial toxicants.
source: Importantly, it provides quantitative evidence that inter-individual variation in mitochondrial genotype can be a factor in determining sensitivity to mitochondrial toxicants.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing haplogroup-specific differences in drug responses

claim: Idiosyncratic responses in DILI are likely due to several small variations coming together to push an individual over the toxicity threshold.
source: It should be noted that idiosyncratic responses in DILI are likely due to several small variations coming together to push an individual over the toxicity threshold.
evidence: Speculation about the multifactorial nature of iDILI

claim: Ten healthy volunteers donated blood for platelet isolation, five from haplogroup H and five from haplogroup J.
source: Ten healthy volunteers were recalled from the previously established HLA-typed archive to give blood, described in Alfirevic et al., 2012. These volunteers were selected based on their mitochondrial haplogroup (haplogroup H and J) and this genotyping has been described in our previous publication (Ball et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of study cohort and methods

claim: HepG2 cells were depleted of mtDNA by treatment with ethidium bromide (1 µM) for eight weeks to generate rho zero cells.
source: HepG2 cells (ECACC Cat# 85011430, RRID: CVCL_0027) (≤passage 7) were cultured and passaged as required in HepG2 ρ0 cell medium (DMEM/F-12+GlutaMAX supplemented with FBS [10% v/v], Lglutamine [4 mM], sodium pyruvate [1 mM], HEPES [2 mM], and uridine [500 µM]) in the presence of ethidium bromide (EtBr; 1 µM). During this period, EtBr was removed for 48 hr every two weeks to help maintain cell viability. Following eight weeks' exposure, EtBr was removed from a subset of cells for one week before characterization to ensure cells were devoid of mtDNA i.e., were ρ0 cells.
evidence: Description of experimental methods for generating rho zero cells

claim: HepG2 rho zero cells are auxotrophic for pyruvate and uridine.
source: ρ0 cells are auxotrophic for pyruvate and uridine, so the absence of these two constituents was the basis for the selection of successfully fused cells i.e., HepG2 cybrids.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about rho zero cell phenotype

claim: HepG2 wild-type cells had an average doubling time of 26.2 hours.
source: Concordantly, HepG2 WT cells had a similar doubling time in media with or without these additives, averaging 26.2 hr.
evidence: Experimental data from cell growth rate measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: HepG2 rho zero cells had an average doubling time of 27.6 hours when cultured in media containing uridine and pyruvate.
source: In contrast, HepG2 ρ0 cells exhibited no growth without uridine and pyruvate and an average doubling time of 27.6 hr when in media containing these two constituents.
evidence: Experimental data from cell growth rate measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: HepG2 rho zero cells exhibited no growth without uridine and pyruvate.
source: In contrast, HepG2 ρ0 cells exhibited no growth without uridine and pyruvate and an average doubling time of 27.6 hr when in media containing these two constituents.
evidence: Experimental data from cell growth rate measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: All nuclear DNA and mtDNA-encoded subunits of the electron transport chain were present in HepG2 wild-type and cybrid cells.
source: All nuclear DNA and mtDNA-encoded subunits of the electron transport chain which were probed for were present in HepG2 WT and cybrid cells.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2

claim: Rho zero cells did not express the mtDNA-encoded subunit of complex IV.
source: However, ρ0 cells did not express the mtDNA-encoded subunit of complex IV.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2

claim: The alpha subunit of ATP synthase was retained in rho zero cells despite other subunits being encoded in nuclear DNA.
source: Notably, despite all the other subunits being encoded in the nuclear DNA, it was only the alpha subunit of ATP synthase that was retained in the ρ0 cells.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2

claim: The concentrations of drugs used in this study were higher than the reported Cmax of the compounds.
source: The authors also recognize that due to this, the concentrations of drugs used were higher than the reported Cmax of the compounds (flutamide Cmax – 72.2 nM, 2-hydroxyflutamide Cmax – 4.4 µM, bicalutamide 1.7 µM, tolcapone 16.5 µM, and entacapone 3.9 µM) (Schulz et al., 1988; Cockshott, 2004; Khetani et al., 2013).
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental design choice, supported by citations to Schulz et al., 1988; Cockshott, 2004; Khetani et al., 2013

claim: Greater spare respiratory capacity is linked to protection against mitotoxicants.
source: Greater SRC is linked to protection against mitotoxicants, and, therefore, the larger SRC observed in haplogroup H may indicate a potential for haplogroup-specific protection against injury by flutamide.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about spare respiratory capacity

claim: Proton leak is a negative indicator of mitochondrial health.
source: Furthermore, proton leak (PL), a negative indicator of mitochondrial health, was significantly greater in haplogroup J compared with haplogroup H (PL mean difference 1.29 pmol/min/ug protein, 95% CI [0.3, 2.27], p=0.016).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about proton leak

claim: Extracellular flux analysis may provide greater sensitivity for detecting and quantifying comparative differences in mitochondrial dysfunction compared with measuring cellular ATP.
source: Therefore, this demonstrates that extracellular flux analysis may provide greater sensitivity for detecting and quantifying comparative differences in mitochondrial dysfunction compared with measuring cellular ATP (nmoles/µg protein).
evidence: Inference from comparison of results between ATP content assays and extracellular flux analysis

claim: Tolcapone is a chemical uncoupler that binds and transports protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane by simple diffusion.
source: For example, tolcapone is a chemical uncoupler that binds and transports protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane by simple diffusion, in the same manner as carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone (FCCP).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about tolcapone mechanism

claim: Chemical-induced increases in spare respiratory capacity can indicate the early induction of protective mitochondrial response.
source: Chemical-induced increases in SRC can indicate the early induction of protective mitochondrial response, driven by homeostatic mechanisms including increased fusion, increased access to fuels, or increased mitochondrial mass (Marchetti et al., 2020; Valera-Alberni and Canto, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marchetti et al., 2020; Valera-Alberni and Canto, 2018

claim: This study created 10 cybrid cell lines, each containing distinct mitochondrial genotypes of haplogroup H or haplogroup J backgrounds.
source: This study created 10 cybrid cell lines, each containing distinct mitochondrial genotypes of haplogroup H or haplogroup J backgrounds.
evidence: Description of study design and outcomes

claim: Haplogroup J showed increased susceptibility to inhibition by flutamide, 2-hydroxyflutamide, and tolcapone.
source: Haplogroup J showed increased susceptibility to inhibition by flutamide, 2-hydroxyflutamide, and tolcapone, via effects on selected mitochondrial complexes (I and II), and an uncoupling of the respiratory chain.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from multiple assays

source: This work was supported by the Centre for Drug Safety Science supported by the Medical Research Council, United Kingdom (Grant Number G0700654); and GlaxoSmithKline as part of an MRC-CASE studentship (grant number MR/L006758/1).
evidence: Statement of funding sources

source: This work was supported by the Centre for Drug Safety Science supported by the Medical Research Council, United Kingdom (Grant Number G0700654); and GlaxoSmithKline as part of an MRC-CASE studentship (grant number MR/L006758/1).
